svg.title: Bench breadboard layout — Teensy board and sensor board
svg.desc: Two half-size breadboards wired for bench bring-up. The upper board carries the Teensy 4.1 straddling the centre channel, with 10k pull-ups and 1nF capacitors on the two quadrature inputs and 4.7k pull-ups on the I2C pair. The lower board carries the two TO-92 Hall latches and the AS5600 breakout. Six jumpers link the two boards. Below, the jumper list and the rules that make the bench mirror the vehicle.
svg.text: Bench layout — two breadboards, six jumpers between them
Pin numbers are provisional — 04-firmware has not pinned them yet, which is exactly why this stage is on a breadboard.

Before you push a single wire in
The TO-92 pin order is not guessable. Legs 1-2-3 are
drawn here as VCC · GND · OUT, which is the common
arrangement — read the DRV5013 datasheet and
confirm it. Reversed VCC/GND destroys the part, which
is why fourteen are spare.
Keep them in the labelled bag until fitted. TI marks a
TO-92 body with an abbreviated code, so loose parts are
unidentifiable and BC looks exactly like AG.
Bend the legs to 2.54 mm before inserting — TO-92 legs
leave the package closer together than that.
The AS5600 breakout may have its own pull-ups fitted.
If it does, the 4.7 kΩ on board A are in parallel — fine.
The six jumpers between the boards

g.text: red + 3.3 V rail A → + rail B
blue − GND rail A → − rail B

svg.text: On board A, five components and nothing else
2 × 10 kΩ — pins 0 and 1 up to the + rail
2 × 1 nF — pins 0 and 1 down to the − rail
2 × 4.7 kΩ — pins 18 and 19 to the + rail
Three rules that make the bench mirror the vehicle
1 · Power VIN from a UBEC, not from USB
Once VUSB–VIN is cut, USB carries data only and the board
will not run on it. Cut it before the first bench session that
involves a UBEC — two supplies fighting is the thing the cut
exists to prevent, and "we'll do it later" is how they meet.
2 · One ground, and check it with a meter
Both boards' − rails tied together, once. On the vehicle this
becomes the star at the motor driver. Beep the two − rails
before powering up — a missing ground reads as a dead sensor.
3 · Nothing on these boards may carry coil current
No relay, no MOSFET, no 12 V. That circuit goes straight onto
soldered perfboard — 600 mA through spring clips, and a
floating gate chatters the relays. Signal here, authority there.
What to prove here, in this order — each step fails for a different reason
1 · Power only. 5 V at VIN, then meter the + rail on board B: 3.3 V. If it is not there, the fault is a jumper, not a sensor.
2 · Hall latches, with a multimeter before any code. Probe each OUT against GND and pass a magnet by. It should
snap between 0 V and 3.3 V and STAY there when the magnet leaves — that is what makes it a latch. If it returns
on its own you have a switch, not a latch, and the whole quadrature scheme is wrong. Flip the magnet to reset it.
3 · I²C scan. Address 0x36 must appear. Nothing else should — one device per bus is the design.
4 · AGC. Read register 0x1A with the magnet at its working gap and tune until it sits mid-scale, then
write that gap down — it is the number the other two vehicles get built to.
5 · Counts last. Only now bring up the quadrature decoder and move a magnet past both latches in sequence.
Counting up one way and down the other is the first proof the (n + ½) spacing is right, and it is cheap to check
here and expensive to check on a wheel.
Steps 1–3 need no firmware beyond a scan sketch. If something is wrong, it is wrong before any code is blamed.
